doc.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Bringing Earl Hines back at the Little Theater in 1964
summary: Dance suggested Hines to Morgenstern and Himmelstein, the concert was a sensation, and Dance became his unofficial manager during the Russian tour.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: of course a lot of those musicians didn’t have the education that white musicians had had. They were probably not good readers to start with. So that was why Basie’s thing stressed head arrangements, which they sort of cooked up themselves. But you know if you take the best black bands of the swing era, from the point of swinging they are undoubtedly very much superior. But you can take Goodman’s band, it’s probably the best of the white bands, Artie Shaw’s, Glenn Miller’s, Tommy Dorsey had a very good band. But in my opinion, I think there was a big difference. But on the other hand you have to take into consideration the way white musicians, you can play and think perhaps more in tune with the white audience. You know that’s more, you’ve got a sound thing there that is more applicable to what white ears are accustomed to. Certainly I mean I can remember my father and mother when they had the plunger muted trumpet and trombone. In Duke’s band they thought that was crazy. The other thing, the other two things I will tell you would be I mentioned Earl Hines in ‘64 I think it was, my friend Dan Morgenstern and his friend David Himmelstein, they got to the Little Theater in New York, and there was an Israeli company playing there. And they couldn’t play on a Saturday or Sunday or something. And Dan and David had got this theater where they could perform jazz. And they opened with Coleman Hawkins and had a big success. And we were talking afterwards and they said, about whom they should have next, and I said well why don’t you get Earl Hines, he’d been through the previous winter with a rather poor little band. I said bring him in and have him play a lot of piano. And they said “would he come?” And I said well I could try. I’d been in touch with him for years, because I had a friend in San Francisco who used to send me records of his broadcasts, and then he used to send me, he had a radio program and he’d tape it. Instead of sending me a letter he’d tape the thing and send it and usually play a number on it, so I knew he was still wonderful. So he came and played a concert in the Little Theater which was a sensation. And it got splendid publicity in New York — Whitney Balliet put it up in the New Yorker and then he made records with Columbia and Victor. And then he was off — he went to Russia for the State Department and for the rest of his life — oh when he went to Russia, he said, “While I’m away, will you take care of any business coming in?” And I always remember we were in a hotel room he took me. He was from Chicago, and he took a gun out of his pocket dropped it across the bed and said, “You better keep this, I better not take that on the State Department tour.” It was loaded, too. So after that I became like his unofficial manager. And you know he made — oh he must have made about thirty albums before he died, and he proved himself, no question about that. I mean he was unlike some of the other famous record makers, he was a genuine improviser. Most things were one take you know.
